12.0.0.en: The celebration of the Jewish Passover was on the 14th of Nisan (April), and therefore Christ's arrival at Bethany (house of affliction) was on the Friday after sunset, which is reckoned as the Sabbath. The supper feast was in the house of Simon the leper, whom the Lord Jesus had healed (Mt 26:6; Mk 14:3). And St. John mentioned the presence of Lazarus at this feast, as an affirmation of his resurrection, and also his sister Martha, who came to help and serve at this supper.

12.1.0.en: As for Mary, the sister of Martha, she brought a flask of perfume of a mina, which is the Roman pound, and is equivalent to about a third of a kilogram or a third of a liter. Spikenard is among the costly perfumes mentioned in the Song of Songs, and it was a source of pride for whoever owned it because of its quality and high price. It was common in honoring the great to pour a little perfume on the head. But what Mary did surpassed many, for she used the most costly perfume of all, and was not content with the head only, but also the feet of the Lord, which shows her love and her gratitude for what the Lord Jesus had done in raising her brother, and she also showed humility by wiping His feet with her hair. And the house's being filled with the fragrance is evidence of the quality of this kind of perfume, and also of the abundance of the quantity Mary used.

12.1.1.en: Beloved, what Mary offered was not perfume, but a loving and humble heart; and God does not accept an offering from a person if it is empty of love and humility (1 Cor 13). Therefore, He rejected the prayer of the Pharisee, and accepted the prayer of the tax collector. For God, in His riches, does not need our offerings at all. But in His love for us, He also rejoices in our love. So take care, beloved, before you offer time or anything to God, that you offer a loving heart and a humble mind, so that God may accept what you offer.

12.2.0.en: In (Mt 26:8, 9; Mk 14:4, 5), the Evangelists mentioned that some objection occurred to Mary's action. But John makes clear that the instigator of this objection was Judas, and makes clear the cause of his objection, revealing the real reason, which is that he was the thief of the money box and a betrayer of trust, and although he claimed otherwise, pretexting the service of the poor, he revealed nothing but his anger at the loss of this sum from under his hands. And on the other hand, St. John reveals to us that the value of this perfume was 300 denarii, and it was known that a laborer's wage for a day was one denarius (Mt 20:10), that is, what Mary offered was the wage of a man for about a year.

12.3.0.en: Christ did not intend any diminishing of the service of the poor (v. 8), but He said this to answer the objector, whose intentions He knew well on the one hand, and so as not to belittle the value of the work of love offered by Mary to His person on the other. Therefore, we find that the Lord began His words by saying "Let her alone," in the plural form, that is, the objection that Judas expressed was agreed with by most of those sitting. And the phrase "against the day of my burying" was a prophetic reference to the coming events, although those present did not understand it. And some see that Christ is pointing out that the journey of death had actually begun with His visit to Bethany, and His last ascent to Jerusalem.

12.4.0.en: Lazarus, raised from the dead, became the strongest evidence that the Lord Jesus is the expected Christ. Therefore, St. John points out that this living evidence was the reason for many Jews coming to Bethany, to see and behold this one raised from the dead. And John also makes clear the extent of the evil to which the chief priests had come in that they wanted to kill an innocent man, Lazarus, to be rid of this conclusive proof, instead of believing and having faith in the person of Christ the Savior.

12.4.1.en: O my God, can the evil heart to this extent overturn the truths, and be led along behind its hatreds?! I beg You, Lord, keep far from us and from all Your people all the wars of the evil one, which toy with minds and hearts, making us blind unjust judges.

12.4.2.en: (2) The entry of Christ into Jerusalem (vv. 12-19):

12.4.3.en: 12- On the next day much people that were come to the feast, when they heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem, 13- Took branches of palm trees, and went forth to meet him, and cried, "Hosanna: Blessed is the King of Israel that cometh in the name of the Lord."

12.4.4.en: 14- And Jesus, when he had found a young ass, sat thereon; as it is written, 15- "Fear not, daughter of Sion: behold, thy King cometh, sitting on an ass's colt." 16- These things understood not his disciples at the first: but when Jesus was glorified, then remembered they that these things were written of him, and that they had done these things unto him. 17- The people therefore that was with him when he called Lazarus out of his grave, and raised him from the dead, bare record. 18- For this cause the people also met him, for that they heard that he had done this miracle. 19- The Pharisees therefore said among themselves, "Perceive ye how ye prevail nothing? behold, the world is gone after him."

12.5.0.en: The celebration of the reception can be reviewed with (Mt 21:1-11; Mk 11:1-11).

12.5.1.en: "The next day": it is the day of Sunday, and the coming of Christ had become known to the crowds, who were the Jews of Jerusalem, Galilee and beyond the Jordan, without doubt, and it was information whose source was everyone who attended or passed on the news at Simon's feast in the house at Bethany.

12.5.2.en: "Branches of palm trees": it was the custom for the common people to receive leaders victorious in wars with palm branches, as an expression of their joy and exultation at salvation and victory. And this great festal procession had the effect of hastening the events of the cross, because of the pain it caused to the chief priests and Pharisees.

12.5.3.en: "Hosanna" means "save us." But this does not necessarily mean the crowd's faith that the Lord Jesus is the Redeemer Christ, but perhaps some saw in Him a teacher and prophet worthy of honor, and others believed He was a political savior who would free the Jewish nation from the Romans.

12.6.0.en: St. John did not concentrate on the details of obtaining the colt as the other Evangelists mentioned it, but was content with the general depiction of the scene of Christ's entry into Jerusalem. He also refers in (v. 15) to the prophecy concerning Christ's riding the colt in (Zech 9:9) without detailing it, unlike St. Matthew in (21:5), because St. John concentrates more on the saving, theological side of the events, and not the historical. As for St. Matthew, his Gospel was directed to the Jewish nation, so he had to elaborate, and link more with the prophecies of the Old Testament that prophesy about the person of Christ, to prove His identity.

12.7.0.en: The meaning is that at the time of Christ's entry into Jerusalem and His riding the colt, it was not in the disciples' minds that this was the same scene that Zechariah had seen and prophesied 500 years before. But when Jesus was glorified, they understood its meaning after His resurrection and ascension, and it also means after the descent of the Holy Spirit on the disciples, by whose descent the eyes of their hearts were opened, so they discovered and linked all the prophecies of the Old Testament with the events of Christ's life on earth, and His saving work.

12.8.0.en: St. John makes clear the strongest reason for the joy of the crowds and their thronging to receive the Lord Jesus, which was the crowds' testimony and affirmation that He had raised Lazarus from the tomb. And on the other hand, he brings us to what was going on in the hearts and minds of the Pharisees of hatred, as they provoked one another to the necessity of acting to confront that One whom everyone had gone after. And instead of making sure and following the truth, their fear of losing their standing as teachers with a position among the people was their greatest concern.

12.9.0.en: What is meant here by the Greeks is not the Gentile idol worshippers, but they were either Gentile proselytes to Judaism, or Jews who had lived for a long time in the land of Greece, and had gone up to Jerusalem to offer sacrifices in the Temple, and to celebrate the Passover. And we understand that what they had heard about the person of the Lord Jesus and His miracles and teachings was the reason for their seeking Him until they found one of His disciples, who was Philip, who in turn informed Andrew, and both went to Christ to inform Him of the Greeks' desire.

12.10.0.en: Christ's answer here was to the two disciples, and also to the Greeks and the listening crowd, and was the beginning of the prediction of the nearness of the salvation that Christ offers. And since their thoughts were confined to the kingdom and earthly glory, Christ began His discourse with what was in their minds, in order to raise them to spiritual understanding. And the expression "that the Son of man should be glorified" means the declaration of His first heavenly glory, which was hidden by the Incarnation. And the way this glory is declared is the cross, then the Resurrection, then the Ascension.

12.11.0.en: This verse is a clarification of the way the Son of Man is glorified, so the Lord Christ used here the parable of the grain of wheat, which points to Him in His Incarnation, for all the glory and value of this grain is in its being buried in the soil and being enveloped by the death of the earth, so what people see as the death of the grain of wheat is the source of life itself, since it will rise and live from its death. And when it rises, it is a source of satisfaction and life for all who feed on it. And this is what Christ wanted to make clear to the crowds, by the efficacy of His death and His granting salvation to everyone who accepts His redemption on the cross, and eats His Body in Communion.

12.12.0.en: After Christ spoke about Himself, He directs a general spiritual teaching, which is considered one of the laws of the Christian life, for every rise to a higher spiritual level requires a loss in material things, which are the lesser, for eternal life with all its glory and splendor requires sacrificing everything that hinders reaching it. So if the body, or the various lusts of the soul, bind a person to the world and make him lose heaven, then the person must resist, and even sacrifice anything, even his life itself, for the permanent and eternal inheritance; and this is what the Lord Christ meant by the word "loseth it." And this faith is what made our fathers the holy martyrs go forward to death with utmost courage and indifference to the might of rulers; for whoever places eternal life before his eyes fears nothing.

12.13.0.en: That is, whoever wants to be a true Christian, and a disciple and servant of Christ's commandment, must follow his Lord and Teacher in all that He did. So if the Lord gave Himself and put Himself to death for the redemption of others, then the faithful servant must imitate Him. And Christ also linked that to the reward, which is the permanent presence of the faithful Christian in the bosom of his Lord, and the honoring of him by the heavenly Father. And we do not think there is any language or conception that brings near to us the meaning of this eternal honor, unlimited by time or size, except trust in all that the Lord Christ says, that whatever a man leaves here, or bears for the sake of Christ, has this reward and this honor. (4) Christ speaks about His death and its effects (vv. 27-36):

12.13.1.en: 27- Now is my soul troubled; and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour: but for this cause came I unto this hour. 28- Father, glorify thy name. Then came there a voice from heaven, saying, "I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again." 29- The people therefore, that stood by, and heard it, said that it thundered: others said, "An angel spake to him." 30- Jesus answered and said, "This voice came not because of me, but for your sakes. 31- Now is the judgment of this world: now shall the prince of this world be cast out. 32- And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me." 33- This he said, signifying what death he should die. 34- The people answered him, "We have heard out of the law that Christ abideth for ever: and how sayest thou, The Son of man must be lifted up? who is this Son of man?" 35- Then Jesus said unto them, "Yet a little while is the light with you. Walk while ye have the light, lest darkness come upon you: for he that walketh in darkness knoweth not whither he goeth. 36- While ye have light, believe in the light, that ye may be the children of light." These things spake Jesus, and departed, and did hide himself from them.

12.14.0.en: What is meant by the soul here is the center of emotional feelings. Christ knows the hour of His crucifixion and death and its nearness, but as a perfect man, He expresses His human feelings by being troubled, for He is between two important matters: a matter that the ordinary human soul rejects, which is the death to which He will submit in order to accomplish our redemption, and then conquer it by His resurrection to accomplish our salvation, and what the righteous spirit, subject to the heavenly Father in His plan, wills. Therefore, the second part of the verse was "What shall I say... save me from this hour?" as though the spirit knows, and answers and strengthens the soul against its emotion, affirming that for the sake of this hour, on which all mankind depends, Christ came.

12.15.0.en: St. Chrysostom and Augustine say that the will of the Son is the glorification of the name of the Father, and the way is death and suffering and the redemption of perishing mankind, and leading them to heaven, so that they glorify the name of the Father on earth, and then in heaven, with eternal glorification, and the Father replies to the Son: "I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again," and its meaning is that through the life of Christ and His repeated witness about the Father, and His teachings about the mysterious relationship between them, and His performing miracles, the Son glorified the Father in this way, and the Father glorified His only-begotten Son by bearing witness to Him also. For the Father declared the glory of the Son:

12.15.3.en: Third: in this verse, "I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again."

12.15.4.en: For the glory between the Father and the Son is one and mutual glory (ch. 13:31, 32; 14:13).

12.15.5.en: "And will glorify it again": it means Christ's ascension into heaven.

12.15.6.en: As for the crowd, when they heard this voice, some believed, because of the surprise and the unexpectedness, that it was the sound of thunder; while others, who distinguished the words, thought it was the voice of an angel from heaven.

12.16.0.en: Christ answered those who thought that an angel was speaking to Him, saying that this voice is for you, that you may believe, for I have no need of it, and I do not doubt the glory of my Father's name or my glory, but it is to remove your doubts toward me.

12.17.0.en: "The judgment of this world": it is not the last judgment, but the judgment of the rejection of Christ, and the judgment of the pagan world, and the judgment of the kingdom of Satan, who held the reins of affairs in the world, so it is the judgment of declaring the iniquity of the whole world.

12.17.1.en: "Cast out": that is, as a result of the first judgment, Satan is bound in his authority over the world, by the crucifixion of Christ, and cast out; and this is what St. Paul explained about Christ's work on the cross toward Satan: "And having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it" (Col 2:15).

12.17.2.en: So Satan has no authority over the children of God who believe in His name and act upon His commandments.

12.18.0.en: "If I be lifted up from the earth": by the cross, hung upon it, I draw all to myself and to the heights.

12.18.1.en: For man without Christ is shackled with the chains of sin and the material life, but with Christ, and in the cross alone, this Crucified One draws all the victims of the evil prince of the world, to take us into His bosom and to His chest upward, that we may be freed from everything that is from below, and enjoy the life with Him that begins here and does not end there.

12.18.2.en: So would that all of us, with firm desire, stretched out our hands to our Christ, our sacrifice, and met with Him at His altar, to take our strength from Him. And then we shall be able to tread the world and Satan under our feet.

12.19.0.en: The crowd faced a difficulty, which was Christ's reference to His death, hung on the cross, on the one hand, and what they had learned from the Law, that the kingdom of Christ is an eternal earthly kingdom (Dan 7:14; Ps 110:4; Isa 9:7), on the other, and the problem is in the mistaken understanding. All the prophecies speak of the eternal spiritual Kingdom of Christ, and not the temporal one. And this is the reason for His saying to Pilate afterward: "My kingdom is not of this world" (ch. 18:36). "Who is this Son of man?": a question of astonishment! For Christ used this expression of Himself repeatedly, and it is the same expression that Daniel used in his prophecy to describe Christ (Dan 7:13). So what do you mean by this usage?! Are you the eternal Christ, or are you an ordinary man liable to death?

12.20.0.en: Christ answered with an indirect answer, pointing to the nearness of His death, describing Himself as the light, which He had said before in (ch. 8:12). And He also urges them to seize the opportunity in holding fast to this light, lest the darkness overtake them through their rejection of this light.

12.20.1.en: And the one who walks in darkness is a lost man who has lost the way and the goal, and this is the case even now for everyone who is far from Christ and His Church. For outside the Church, which is the ship of salvation, there is nothing but the material and intellectual whirlpools of the world, which swallow a person far from the voice of Christ, so he drowns and his spirit is suffocated, while he supposes that he knows the right way and is walking in it. And the result, sadly, is the loss of the salvation of his soul.

12.21.0.en: Christ still urges them to believe in Him, and to make use of the opportunity of His being with them, even if it is short. And He adds also that whoever follows Him in His way, and obeys His commandments, becomes a child of light, that is, bearing the characteristics of the true light, reflecting this light to all around him.

12.21.1.en: So people see in the Christian man righteousness, purity, faithfulness and the rest of the virtues. Are we so? "And departed, and did hide himself from them": it indicates the end of the discourse, and His withdrawing by Himself away from the crowds, as came in (ch. 8:59). And the Lord Jesus was accustomed, during His life on earth, to these spiritual retreats.

12.22.s.en: (5) The reasons for the Jews' unbelief

12.22.0.en: "So many": St. John makes clear the abundance, multiplicity and variety of the miracles that the Lord Jesus performed. And yet most of the Jews did not believe, to make clear the hardness of their hearts. And this expression also indicates astonishment and amazement at the reaction of the Jews to all that the Lord had done.

12.23.0.en: St. John removes from us the astonishment and amazement at the Jews' stance toward Christ, and says to us: had not Isaiah said before that they refused to believe his prophecies, and refused also the arm of the Lord stretched out for salvation? Their present stance in rejecting Christ is no different from their stance in the time of Isaiah in rejecting God and His redemption of His people (Isa 53:1). And St. John also presents in (v. 40) a new prophecy that Isaiah prophesied, which also makes clear the cause of their rejection of Christ.

12.24.0.en: This prophecy is taken from (Isa 6:9, 10), and the Gospels transmitted it with some adaptation (Mt 13:13-15; Mk 4:12; Lk 8:10), and what is meant is not that God is the cause of the hardness of their hearts, but their many murmurings and their rejection of God and not hearing Him are what blinded their eyes and hearts to the works of God in the time of Isaiah, and the miracles and teachings of Christ in His time. Therefore, the responsibility for the rejection falls on the Jews, stiffnecked and hard of heart, after God had exhausted every attempt with them.

12.25.0.en: "Saw his glory": what is meant is the glory of Christ, and the talk returns to the vision of Isaiah (6), in which he saw the glory of God and around Him the cherubim and seraphim crying: "Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory" (v. 3). And since the Holy Bible testifies that no one has seen the Father (ch. 1:18), therefore the One whom Isaiah saw is God the Son, that is, Christ.

12.26.0.en: St. John returns and makes clear that every rule has an exception. For if most of the Jews did not believe in Christ, there were also those who believed in Him from among the council of seventy, which is the highest Jewish council, and its members were called the rulers, and examples of those who believed are Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea, whose faith appeared after the events of the crucifixion. But because of fear of the Pharisees and their religious and social power, no one was able to declare his faith (see ch. 7:3; 9:22; 19:38; 20:19).

12.26.1.en: And St. John also makes clear a reason that makes many deny their faith, or at least not declare it, which is their desire to preserve people's love and praise for them, even if this be at the expense of God. So do not descend, my brother, to these relationships or bargains, out of love for a position or honor, and remember the saying of Peter and the Apostles that "We ought to obey God rather than men" (Acts 5:29), whatever the temptation, or whatever the threat.

12.27.s.en: (6) The judgment of unbelief in Christ

12.27.0.en: "Jesus cried": that was in another place, but on the same day. And what the Lord would say in these verses came as a summary of what He had said in previous verses, especially (ch. 5; 7; 8; 10), and its summary is His oneness with the Father who sent Him, for faith in the Son is faith in the Father, and denial of one is denial of the other. And Christ adds that whoever has seen Him has seen the Father, because the two are one in divinity (ch. 14:9), and this is strong evidence of equality; for who of mankind, or of the greatest prophets of the Jews, or of the archangels, dares to declare that he is the visible image of the Father, other than Christ, to Him be glory? Because He is: the imprint of the Father's essence, as St. Paul describes Him in the Epistle to the Hebrews (3).

12.28.0.en: This is what Christ had already declared in (ch. 8:12) (see the commentary). We can also summarize the saying in that Christ is the only light of the world, and apart from Him there is nothing but destructive darkness and the ignorance of error. And the light of Christ is a light of experience in the life of all His holy children, for talking about the light of Christ is one thing and living within it is another.

12.29.0.en: "I came not to judge the world": (see ch. 8:15) the purpose of my Incarnation now is not punishment or judgment, but the salvation of the world, on condition of faith in me and acting upon my commandments; for the judgment of mankind is connected with the Second Coming of the Lord Christ.

12.30.0.en: But those who reject my words, or faith in me, will have a great judgment. And every word and teaching and work that I performed and they did not accept will be a witness against them in their condemnation.

12.30.1.en: And this makes clear to all of us that divine judgment is not by partiality or for chosen ones to the exclusion of others, but has a standard, which is faith in the words of Christ and acting upon them as far as possible, in a life of spiritual striving that knows no weariness.

12.31.0.en: (See the explanation of 5:30; 7:16-18) For the Father is the source of everything, and the Son is the means of His declaration and communication, and the two are one in essence and equal.

12.32.0.en: "And I know": and Christ's knowledge here surpasses all human knowledge. Therefore, what He declares is all the truth, that is, the way to reach eternity is acting upon the commandment and living by it. For theoretical faith does not save its possessor, and what is its use if it is not turned into a life lived.

12.32.1.en: And these words are for all of us, for Christianity is not a set of obligations, but the obedience of the love of God in His commandment, and whoever endures the toil of carrying out the commandment, Christ gives him the experience of the pledge of eternal life, here on earth, according to the riches of the work of His grace in us.

12.32.2.en: The washing of the feet; the foretelling of Judas' betrayal; Peter's denial
